newsitem.title: GERMANY: Huge Telekom share offer cheaper than expected.
newsitem.headline: Huge Telekom share offer cheaper than expected.

text.p: German phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG said Sunday it would raise as much as 20 billion marks ($13.28 billion) from its share issue, the largest ever in Europe, and sweetened the deal by pricing shares well below expectations.

Company officials said the issue was oversubscribed at least five times and that the stock offering had whipped up such huge demand from private investors that its success was bound to help boost broad share holding in Germany.

Telekom Chief Executive Ron Sommer told a news conference in Frankfurt the issue price for the share offer was 28.50 marks ($18.92) and that after the share launch some 26 percent of the state-owned company's capital would be in private hands.
"This price is in line with the market. It creates a good foundation for bourse trade that begins tomorrow and aims to create a stable and lasting relationship to our shareholders," Sommer said.
"With this volume of proceeds, our flotation is Europe's biggest ever and the second biggest in the world," he added.
The world's largest listing was the initial public offering of Japan's Nippon Telegraph & Telephone Corp.

Shares in Deutsche Telekom begin trading for the first time Monday in Germany and New York, where they will be issued at $18.89, and a day later in Tokyo. Analysts expect shares to begin trading in Frankfurt at around 33 marks ($21.90), giving investors an instant 4.5 mark ($2.99) profit on paper.

Telekom, Europe's largest telephone company with annual sales of 66 billion marks ($48.8 billion), will issue a total of 713 million shares. This includes the allotment of 600 million shares, an overallotment of another 90 million shares and up to 30 million shares for employees.

Two-thirds of the total issue would be placed in Germany and 33 percent abroad, with the largest chunk going to North and South America. More than half the issue would be taken up by institutional investors, pension funds and other professionals.
But nearly two million ordinary Germans joined Telekom's offering, marking a turning point as more Germans turn away from safe investments in bonds to more risky stock investment.

These small shareholders, wooed by Telekom in alluring television advertising, are being guaranteed a minimum of 100 shares each and would take up 315 million shares of the total. Many would also get a discount of 50 pfennigs (33 cents) a share and be eligible for loyalty bonuses if they keep their shares.
Telekom shares will immediately take a dominant role in Germany's 30-share DAX stock market index.
Nicole Cousins, telecoms analyst at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, said she believed the lower-than-expected price for the issue meant there was a good chance of price gains.
"We thought it would come in at the high end of the range (30 marks)" she said. "Based on our benchmarks we thought it was fairly valued at 30 marks ($19.91)."

Jonathan Shantry, European telecoms analyst for Credit Lyonnais in London, said the pricing guaranteed a good value for small investors because the return would be close to the 6 percent offered by German bonds.
"There is room for more gains. The share price could go up to around 33 marks, at which point institutions will probably begin taking profits," he said. "The fair value is 30 marks."
Telekom AG said it would use the proceeds from the issue to strengthen its balance sheet by paying off outstanding debt, an issue that was a concern particularly to foreign investors.
Ronaldo Schmitz, board member of Deutsche Bank, the lead manager of the issue, said German banks hoped to build on the momentum from Telekom's offering to encourage share investment.
"We cannot let this chance get away," he said.
